name: Capacity and Layered Programs
blurb:
The most important number in data centre insurance is not a premium. It is the gap between what a campus is worth and what the market can write.

S&P Global Ratings puts total insurable value for a single hyperscale campus at 20 to 30 billion dollars. For comparison, limits on a bridge or tunnel typically run 5 to 10 billion. Munich Re offers up to roughly 250 million in net capacity for one data centre construction project. Reaching 10 billion on a single site means layering a tower across forty or more carriers.

The consequence is that full cover is often not purchasable at any price. Zurich reports many projects insured for one third to one half of total value. The rest sits on the owner's balance sheet, whether or not anyone has described it that way to the lender.

This page tracks the capacity position itself: what carriers will write, how towers are structured, where the uninsured remainder lands, and what underwriters now demand before they will put out their largest limits.

points.desc: S&P Global Ratings estimates total insurable value for a single hyperscale campus at 20 to 30 billion dollars, and notes construction-phase valuations reaching 30 billion. Traditional infrastructure such as bridges and tunnels typically carries 5 to 10 billion in limits.
points.name: A campus is worth more than the market can insure

points.desc: Munich Re offers up to roughly 250 million dollars of net capacity on a single data centre construction project. Reaching 10 billion on one site therefore means a structured tower across forty or more carriers, with lead underwriters setting terms and following markets supplying capacity.
points.name: One carrier writes about 250 million

points.desc: Zurich, in Data Center Risks Right Now: 2026 US Edition, reports that many projects carry insurance for only one third to one half of total value. The difference is uninsured exposure sitting on somebody balance sheet, which is a financing question as much as a risk one.
points.name: Many projects are insured for a third to a half of value

points.desc: Brokers report large programs topping out around 3.5 billion dollars against projects worth roughly ten times that. Aon expanded its Data Center Lifecycle Insurance Program to 3.5 billion in April 2026, adding a billion of capacity and extending it to facilities entering long-term operation.
points.name: Placed limits top out near 3.5 billion

points.desc: S&P counts roughly 11,000 data centres in operation globally, an insurable asset base above two trillion dollars, generating perhaps 10 billion in new premium in 2026, about twice the global aviation insurance market. Swiss Re projects the pool growing from about 10.6 billion to 24.2 billion by 2030.
points.name: The asset base is over two trillion and the premium pool is doubling

points.desc: Bracewell notes the consequence policyholders discover after a loss: a major claim triggers coverage across several policies with different wordings, different claims-handling protocols and different coverage positions. The structure that makes the limit purchasable also makes the recovery contested.
points.name: A layered tower is harder to claim against

points.desc: Builders risk terminates at substantial completion, leaving an equipment-loaded campus to be picked up by a separate operational property program. The seam between the two is a structural gap, and lifecycle programs exist specifically to cover the transition.
points.name: Builders risk ends before operations begin

points.desc: Swiss Re modelling finds more than a quarter of US data centre capacity in areas facing three or more large-hail days a year, and over 40 percent in zones with significant to very high tornado risk. Zurich reports 64 percent of capacity under construction in 2026 sits outside traditional hubs such as Northern Virginia.
points.name: Siting has moved into weather that underwriters price

points.desc: A 500 MW operational facility is a single point of loss capable of generating a claim larger than a major hurricane on one carrier book. Underwriters are beginning to manage data centre aggregation the way they manage catastrophe aggregation, and concentration surcharges are emerging.
points.name: Aggregation is being managed like catastrophe exposure

points.desc: Broker commentary describes carriers applying sub-limits to business interruption arising from cooling or technology failure, well below the property limit. The specific figures circulating are not yet traceable to a named carrier or filing, and are held here until they are.
points.name: To verify: the sub-limit position on business interruption

points.desc: The tenant that owns the accelerators buys a separate electronic data processing floater rather than relying on the operator property policy. Reported limits and the point at which underwriters demand spatial separation are not yet confirmed against a named market source.
points.name: To verify: tenant equipment floater limits and concentration terms

summary: A hyperscale campus can carry 20 to 30 billion dollars of insurable value. The largest net capacity a single carrier will put on one construction project is around 250 million. That arithmetic, not any particular peril, is the binding constraint on the AI buildout.
